subject: computer-science

moments.title: Cook's theorem
moments.body: Cook proves the Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT) is NP-complete: every problem in NP can be reduced to SAT in polynomial time. This defines a class of problems that all rise or fall together — solve one efficiently, solve them all.
moments.takeaway: Computer science gained a tool for proving problems hard without proving them impossible.

moments.title: Karp's 21 NP-complete problems
moments.body: Karp's paper 'Reducibility Among Combinatorial Problems' shows 21 well-known problems are NP-complete: travelling salesman, graph colouring, knapsack, Hamiltonian cycle, vertex cover. Within a few years hundreds of NP-complete problems are catalogued (Garey and Johnson, 1979).
moments.takeaway: The NP-complete class explained why so many practically important problems seemed to resist efficient solution.

now.title: Complexity today
now.body: P vs NP remains the most famous open problem in computer science. The Clay Mathematics Institute offers $1 million for a solution; it is one of seven Millennium Prize problems. Most researchers believe P ≠ NP. Modern cryptography would collapse if P = NP.
now.open_questions: Does P equal NP? Quantum complexity (BQP) adds new classes. Average-case complexity matters more than worst-case for practical algorithms.

reflection: Donald Knuth offered to pay $0.32 for any answer to P vs NP — a hexadecimal pound — but specified he was betting on P = NP. He has lost no money so far.
